30:4.1.1.text: You found it. Sit on the bench, not the step. The step's where people stand when they want me to notice them. Good. Now we're two old fools looking at a parking lot. Nobody looks twice at that.

30:4.1.2.text: Front tonight. You'll hear it in the poplars first.

30:4.1.3.text: Where'd you go? Don't tell me where. Tell me the wind.

30:4.1.4.text: That's the third time that truck's gone by. No. Different truck. Never mind.

30:4.1.5.text: You've got Bald Eagle on your boots. Wipe them before you go in the store.

30:4.1.6.text: Two days of that. Creek'll be running.

30:4.1.7.text: You've been noticed. Don't look at the lot. You've been noticed, that's all.

30:4.1.8.text: You've got a face on you like you found something. Put it away. Talk about fish.

30:4.1.9.text: Boreal Range. We said the outfit. We drilled the gabbro south of the Kawishiwi, winters off the roads, summers on the pads. Core in the boxes, boxes on the truck. Nobody asked.

30:4.1.10.text: Gabbro. Bald Eagle. The country south of them to the road. That's all in the state's files. I'm not telling you anything.

30:4.1.w1.text: Tauno: the crews drilled south of the Kawishiwi, around Gabbro and Bald Eagle.

30:4.1.c3.text: What did you do for them?

30:4.1.11.text: Cut line. Hauled core. Nine years. I never wrote anything for them. Paid for my house.

30:4.1.12.text: Same reason anybody comes here. Something under the ground somebody in the Cities wanted. Mining's not the problem. Men are the problem. Same as anything.

30:4.1.c5.if: the player carries the pack, or asks about the patch

30:4.1.13.text: Crew packs were numbered. The office stencilled them so nobody walked off with one. Fourteen was Walt's, from '71. Walt walked off with one.

30:4.1.c6.if: the notebook's "Two Stump" is on the Walt page and not yet inked

30:4.1.15.text: Huh. Gabbro. The drill-road landing on the south shore. We cut two stumps square at the landing in '75 to tie off the sledges for the winter road. Walt called it that? He would.

30:4.1.c9.if: the notebook's "V.'s water" is on the Walt page and not yet inked

30:4.1.17.text: V. Veli. Brother. That's Bald Eagle, then. Where they found Eino. He never wrote Eino's name, did he. No. He wouldn't.

30:4.1.18.text: He swam better than Walt. Everybody knew that. Ask anybody who grew up on our street.

30:4.1.19.text: To go to the papers. He said it in the core shed like he was saying he wanted a sandwich. Walt told him to wait. You know how that went.

30:4.1.20.text: Ollie Pekkala. Drag line, nine days in. Ollie walks the long portage up by Stuart now, evenings, since his wife. He'll tell you or he won't.

30:4.1.w2.text: Ollie Pekkala found Eino. Walks the Stuart Portage evenings.

30:4.1.21.text: A truck crew. Ours. That's enough on that today. Come back when you've been somewhere.

30:4.1.w3.text: Eino's canoe was found by a Boreal truck crew. Tauno stopped talking when I asked.

30:4.1.22.text: Walt didn't drown. I've thought that since the day I heard.

30:4.1.23.text: Birch Lake. South shore. With a southerly blowing, the way I heard it. I know an upwind canoe when I hear of one. So would anybody who stood on Bald Eagle in '77.

30:4.1.w4.text: Tauno: Walt's canoe was found on Birch's south shore in a southerly. 'Upwind.' Same as Eino's.

30:4.1.c16.text: Why would he do it that way?

30:4.1.24.text: So some of us would know. Don't ask me who 'us' is.

30:4.1.25.text: Who said he went anywhere? I said he didn't drown. Those are different things.

30:4.1.26.text: Len Saari. Nice man. Ask him anything, he'll ring it for you.

30:4.1.27.text: Don't tell Len where you're going next. He's a nice man. Thursdays he has lunch. Has for fifty years.

30:4.1.28.text: With the office. Watch the dock on a Thursday. Quarter to twelve. You'll see a boat nicer than my house.

30:4.1.w5.text: Tauno says Len has lunch on Thursdays 'with the office'. Watch the dock, 11:45.

30:4.1.c20.if: the player has seen Mary at the window, or asks about the office

30:4.1.29.text: Mary typed for the office. Tuesdays and Fridays she's in there with bars. Ask her about Leo. Not the office. Leo was her husband. He drilled.

30:4.1.c21.if: after the crews' landing, and at least one porch visit since 1.3

30:4.1.30.text: You went to the landing. Good. Now go up the grade. South-west, till it quits, then keep on the way it was going. The west pads. The big one's in a hollow, the Kettle. Go after a rain. Two days of it. Then tell me if the creek still runs orange.

30:4.1.c22.text: What would it mean if it does?

30:4.1.31.text: Means rock doesn't change its mind. Go after a rain.

30:4.1.32.text: My knees. And I know what it looks like.

30:4.1.c24.if: asked by the player, on the porch

30:4.1.33.text: Don't tell me. I'm old. I talk in my sleep.

30:4.1.35.text: If anybody asks, I told you the walleye are deep. Which they are.

30:4.1.36.text: Catch anything? Say yes. Say you got a walleye off the reef. Somebody's listening.

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.1.text: You're the one with the old crew pack. Len. Len Saari. I was with the crews, back when. Sit, sit. You want coffee? Kim, get them a coffee.

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.2.text: Oh, we were all over that country. Here, give me your map. I'll ring the old pads for you. That's all public, the state has every bit of it. There's the winter-road grade off Bald Eagle, the west shore. There's the west pads. Most of it's grown in. You'd want boots.

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.3.text: Walt took it hard. You'd have too. Walt was never right after his brother. Nice man. Never right.

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.w1.text: Len: Walt was 'never right'. Denny: they told him Walt 'wasn't well'. Same words.

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.4.text: You've been talking to Tauno. It was an accident. Big lake, October. I was at the funeral. We started the same week, him and me. June of '72. Isn't that funny, the things you keep.

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.w2.text: Len and Eino were hired the same week, 1972.

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.5.text: Oh, nothing up there. Nothing was ever drilled east of Bald Eagle. Waste of a trip, too, the fishing's poor. I'd stay west. West is where the history is.
30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.5.if: the player names any of them

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.w3.text: Len said nothing was ever drilled east of Bald Eagle. E-7's filed on Pietro. That's east.

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.6.text: Little consulting for the new company. Community history, they call it. Old photos, old names. Somebody's got to remember. Matter of fact. You're out that way. Would you take me a picture?

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.c5.if: Len has mentioned his wife once, in the "What do you do now?" follow-up or the café small talk

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.7.text: Elsie's at the home in Ely. Since '19. Good place. Not cheap. I go every day but Thursday.

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.w4.text: Len visits his wife every day but Thursday.

30:4.2/len-saari-first-meeting.8.text: Oh, where to? That's nice. Bring me back a walleye story.

30:4.2.1.1.text: For the open house. The new company wants to show it's been here before, that it's part of things. Which it is. Get me a picture of the old crib at the crews' landing, if it's still standing, and one of a drill casing up on the pads. Any casing. Forty dollars. That's not nothing.

30:4.2/mary-pelto-first-meeting.1.text: Sit down, you're blocking my light. Have a bar. They're lemon. They're not good. Have one anyway.

30:4.2/mary-pelto-first-meeting.2.text: I typed for Boreal nine years. Four hundred words a day for that office and I never read one. That was the job.

30:4.2/mary-pelto-first-meeting.3.text: Leo drilled. He was the best driller on that belt and he'd tell you so himself. He stamped his initials on the end of every box he ever filled, so they'd know whose work it was. With his dad's punch set. Leo said they drilled where they were told and logged what they were told. He said it like a joke.

30:4.2/mary-pelto-first-meeting.c3.text: Are any of his boxes still out there?

30:4.2/mary-pelto-first-meeting.4.text: Oh, I suppose. Out at the pads. Rotten. I'd like a lid. Isn't that foolish. Just a lid, with his letters on it.

30:4.2/mary-pelto-first-meeting.5.text: Loud. Kind. Couldn't sit still in church. Leo used to say the whole country was naturally mineralised, him included, after a Saturday.

30:4.2/mary-pelto-first-meeting.6.text: It was in a report. I typed a lot of reports. I have to get to the bank before noon.

30:4.2/mary-pelto-first-meeting.w1.text: Mary used the words 'naturally mineralised' and then left.

30:4.2/mary-pelto-first-meeting.7.text: The Haapala boys. Walt was the quiet one. Eino was the joker. I'll say that much and that's all I'll say.

30:4.3.1.text: You came in from the lake side? Nobody comes in from the lake side. You're the help. Okay. Tasha. Can you carry a cooler and not drop it in a creek? That's the whole interview.

30:4.3.2.text: Iron, mostly, the colour. What you can't see is the rest. Sulfide rock gets air and water on it and makes acid, and the acid takes the metals out of the rock. Somebody stacked ten thousand tons of it there in 1976 and walked away.

30:4.3.3.text: The old company's. We bought their files. Now it's ours to explain. I'm for the mine if it's done right. That's not a slogan. That's my whole job.

30:4.3.c6.if: always, but it lands harder if the player has heard Tauno's or Mary's lines

30:4.3.4.text: Background means before anybody touched it. What the water was like before there was a pad, or a trench, or us. You measure background so later you can say what you changed.

30:4.3.c7.text: And if somebody calls the trench water background?

30:4.3.5.text: Then they're saying the creek was always like this. That nobody did it. These stations were touched.

30:4.3.w1.text: Tasha: 'background' means before anybody touched it. The creek below the old pad was touched.

30:4.3.6.text: My book. The tablet's the company's. The book's mine.

30:4.3.7.text: Tower. Everybody's dad was at the mine. Mine was. I'm the first geologist in the family and the last one anybody expected. I want a job near home. That's not a crime yet.

30:4.3.8.text: Old Boreal box. Take it if you want it. It's not in anybody's inventory, believe me.

30:4.3.9.text: If anybody asks, you helped a girl from Tower carry her coolers. Which you did. Lake side's faster for you. Go before the wind gets up.

30:4.3.w2.text: The creek below the Kettle pad still runs orange after rain. I saw it.

30:4.3.10.text: Is that an old Boreal box end? We'd love that for the history wall. Forty dollars?

30:4.4.1.text: L.P. Three, seventy-six. That's his punch set. That's his dad's punch set. Sit down. Not there. The back table. The window's for bars.

30:4.4.2.text: I typed it. The water report. The fall of '76. Mr. Brekke pencilled it and I typed it. And I knew it was wrong, because I'd typed the summer one. I never read what I typed. I read that one.

30:4.4.3.text: The creek below the pad. In the summer report it was the creek below the pad. In the fall report it was background. Same water. Different word. Eino pulled the pencilled copy out of the burn barrel the same afternoon. I saw him do it, through the window. I went back to my typing.

30:4.4.4.text: Because you went and got Leo's lid. Nobody's gone anywhere for Leo since 1981.

30:4.4.5.text: If you're looking for what the Haapala boys had, and don't tell me if you are, I don't want to know, then I'll tell you what went missing. In September of '77, Dale Sorensen's book went missing. Green cloth, like a hymnal. He kept it in his truck. Mr. Brekke had the office inside out for three days. Every drawer. My drawer. And the summer before that, Mr. Brekke did his own typing. One night in August. He never did his own typing. My ribbon was moved on in the morning, and my carriage was set wrong.

30:4.4.c3.text: Would you know something typed in that office?

30:4.4.6.text: Anyone would who looked. It was a big grey machine with a tired e. The e sits a hair low. Everything that came out of that office has it, the reports the state has and anything else. If somebody ever had something and wanted to know where it came from. That's all I'm saying.

30:4.4.w1.text: Mary: everything typed in the Boreal office has a low 'e'. The state's 1976 reports have it.

30:4.4.7.text: There's one more thing. I saw Dale's book once. Open. He wrote in it at my desk because his truck was cold. Two letters and a number. L.P. The state man who came on Fridays. The water inspector. His initials were the same as Leo's. And Leo was fighting Mr. Brekke all that winter about the pads, everybody heard it. And I thought: if that book ever comes out, they'll say Leo took money. Leo never took a dime from anybody. He wouldn't take my mother's coffee without paying for it.

30:4.4.w2.text: Mary: 'L.P.' meant two men in that office. Leo Pelto, who drilled, and the state water inspector who came Fridays. Leo took nothing.

30:4.4.c4.text: If it comes out, I'll make sure they know which L.P.

30:4.4.8.text: You can't make sure of anything. But thank you.

30:4.4.c5.text: Then maybe it shouldn't come out.

30:4.4.9.text: That's what I've told myself for fifty years. It's a comfortable thing to tell yourself. It doesn't keep.

30:4.4.10.text: And one more, and then I'm done, and you'll let me eat my bar. That summer, '76, the boys were at a fly camp. The two of them, twelve days. I ran the radio, mornings and nights. 'Ely office, this is Far End.' That was them. The pilot said it was the dead-end bay past Bald Eagle. The one that doesn't go anywhere. The boys called it the far end. Eino's report came in late, in his own hand, and it put the pit on Pietro. I typed Pietro. I remember thinking, that's not what the radio said. Nobody asks the typist.

30:4.4.w3.text: Mary: in Aug 1976 the brothers' fly camp, E-7, answered the radio as 'Far End'. The dead-end bay past Bald Eagle, the one that doesn't go anywhere. Eino's report put it on Pietro.

30:4.4.11.text: I saw Leo's lid on their wall. 'Driller unknown.' Well. At least it's on a wall.

30:4.5.1.text: Well? Kettle pad. That's up by the river, north of Gabbro, isn't it.

30:4.5.c1.text: No. South-west of Bald Eagle. In a hollow.

30:4.5.2.text: That's right. I wanted to see if you went. And?

30:4.5.c3.text: The stones are orange. It wasn't running.

30:4.5.3.text: Fifty years. Rock doesn't change its mind. That's the stain. It never comes out. Go back after a rain sometime if you want to see it run.

30:4.5.5.text: I don't write on maps. That one I didn't write on. The office did. Crew chiefs got one. I was supposed to give it back in '79. I forgot for forty-seven years.

30:4.5.c5.text: E-7 (fly camp) after E.H. field sketch

30:4.5.6.text: Eino's. He set them in '75, walked them every week. One to six above the pad, seven to twelve below. In September '76, seven to twelve became background.

30:4.5.7.text: Means it was like that before anybody came. It wasn't.

30:4.5.w1.text: Tauno: in Sept 1976 stations 7–12 below the Kettle pad were relabelled 'background'.

30:4.5.c9.if: the player has read the map's corner

30:4.5.8.text: I checked maps. Checking's not writing. Every map went past the crew chief. That's what a crew chief was. A man things went past.

30:4.5.9.text: Fly camp. The Haapala boys went in by plane in August '76, twelve days. I was on the west pads the whole month, I never saw it. If it were me looking for an old crew's line, I'd look for orange on the blazes. We dabbed every one so the next man could find it in snow.

30:4.5.c11.text: What does an old test pit look like?

30:4.5.10.text: Like nothing. That's the point of it. Square. A square slump in the ground, a little lower than it should be. Things grow in a square there that don't grow in squares, bunchberry, moss. If it had a lid, the lid's under the moss. And look at the ground on the way to it. Core spill. Chips out of the sample bags. Where a crew walked with bags every day, there's chips. You'd think it was gravel.

30:4.5.w2.text: Tauno: crew blazes have a dab of orange. An old pit is a square slump; bunchberry grows in a square; the lid's under the moss. Core chips mark where a crew walked.

30:4.5.c12.if: after the Pietro visit, §4.7, if the sketch fitted nothing

30:4.5.11.text: Eino drew it? Eino was a joker. He once logged a moose as a station. Station thirteen. It wandered off and Brekke made him do the paperwork. You want to read Eino, turn your head.

30:4.5.w3.text: Tauno: Eino joked in his reports. 'Turn your head.'

30:4.6/the-open-house-fourth.c1.text: The First Look: Boreal Range Minerals, 1970–1984.

30:4.6/the-open-house-fourth.1.text: Leo. Pete the cook. Me, God help me, with hair. Walt. Eino. And that's Len, next to me. 'Names unknown.' He was standing next to me.

30:4.6/the-open-house-fourth.w1.text: The 1975 crew photo at the open house: Walt, Eino, Tauno, Len, Leo. Len captioned it 'names unknown'.

30:4.6/the-thursday-lunch-tier.w1.text: Thursday, 11:45. A varnished launch, an old man with a gold ring. Len takes his line.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.1.text: Carl. Carl Brekke. I ran the old office, God help me, back when the trucks still had running boards. You're the one with Walt's old crew pack.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.2.text: Carl, this is the one I told you about. With the pack.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.3.text: Sit, sit. Len, get them a coffee. You're the one with Walt's old crew pack.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.4.text: Walt was the best line-cutter I ever had. Could put a line through a cedar swamp straight as a rifle. Shame about his brother. Lovely boy. Hothead. Those big lakes in October.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.5.text: Len says you've been asking about Bald Eagle. Lovely lake. Cold.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.6.text: Len says you've been up the old grade. You take a good picture. That's our landing, on the board there. Thank you.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.7.text: Len says you're going to {lake} next. Good walleye on {lake}, if you know where.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.8.text: Len says you're a careful paddler. That's the best thing anybody's said about anyone this summer.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.9.text: Everybody up here was young once and did what the office said. If you ever find what that family thought they had, you'll find it's old paper. Old paper burns.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.10.text: Good. That's what it's for. Len, tell them where the walleye are.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.c2.text: Walt seemed to think it mattered.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.11.text: Walt thought a lot of things mattered. That's what made him a good guide. And a poor sleeper.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.c3.if: Needle; only if Tauno, Maggie or the crew map has given the numbers

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.12.text: I wouldn't know. Len. The check.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.w1.text: I said 'stations seven to twelve' to the ring. His hand went still. 'I wouldn't know.'

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.13.text: Give my best to Tauno. He kept a lovely book.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.14.text: Come by the house sometime. Len knows the way. I've got a launch, I'll give you a ride across. Old men like company.

30:4.6/brekkes-conversation-once-open.15.text: Did he. Did he say that. That's enough for today.

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.1.text: You know. Sit. The boards are dry this end.

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.2.text: Fifty-one years of lunches. Imagine. He helped with Elsie's room. You know what a room costs? I didn't either. I tell him who asked what. That's all. Who asked what. It's nothing, it's just, who asked what.

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.c3.text: How long have you been telling him about me?

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.3.text: Since the first coffee. I rang you the old pads because they're public. I'd have rung them for anybody. And then I'd have told him.

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.c4.if: only if the player has said Eino's name to Len once before

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.4.text: I drove him back from the office. The last Monday in August. Carl had the door shut an hour. Eino didn't say a word, all the way. He asked me to let him out at the Y, and he walked the last mile. I knew he'd been spoken to. Everybody knew. Nobody knew what that meant. I didn't want to.

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.w1.text: Len: on the last Monday of Aug 1977, Brekke had Eino behind a shut door for an hour. Len drove him back. 'Spoken to.'

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.5.text: Tauno's always known. Fifty years he's sat on that porch and I've sat in there. We nod. He's never once said it to my face. Isn't that something. That's how we do it up here.

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.c6.text: Tell him whatever you have to.

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.6.text: That's not forgiveness. No. All right.

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.7.text: You don't have to. He'll know you know. He knows everything eventually. That's his gift.

30:4.6/lens-leak-and-the.8.text: He asked about you Thursday. I said you'd mostly talked about fish. Which you have.

30:4.8.1.text: There's a woman writes for that Duluth paper. The Ledger. She asked the right question once. In 2019. Asked the state for the old creek sheets. Nobody else ever asked. You mind if I call her?

30:4.8.2.text: I'll use the phone at the Legion. Not mine. I'll say somebody's carrying Walt's pack and asking the right questions. That's all I'll say. She'll do the rest or she won't.

30:4.8.3.text: Suit yourself. Somebody'll call her. Somebody always does, eventually.

30:4.8.c3.text: Why don't you talk to her yourself?

30:4.8.4.text: Because I'd have to tell her how I know. Not yet.

30:4.9.1.text: You doing anything this morning? I need a ride to the Little Gabbro road. You drive. My eyes are no good past the junction. I'll buy the gas.

30:4.9.4.text: That one keeps her own book. You can tell by how she carries it. Like Eino.

30:4.9.5.text: Core shed. Thirty by sixty. Stove at that end. Phone on the pole there, a party line, six camps on it, anybody could pick up and listen. People did. Eino called Duluth from that pole. The third of October. Anybody on the line could've heard. Somebody did. I've thought about every man on that line for forty-nine years. I've never said a name and I'm not going to start.

30:4.9.c3.text: You said you never wrote anything for them.

30:4.9.6.text: I said that. September '76. Brekke had me in the office. He had the field books on his desk, Eino's, with the numbers from below the pad. He had his pencil. He said the state wanted a clean book. He said a crew chief who couldn't keep a clean book was a crew chief Minneapolis could replace. I had a house. Irene had picked the curtains. I sat at the table in the core shed, right about here, three nights, and I copied three days of readings into a new book in my own hand. His numbers. My hand. That's the clean book. He's got it somewhere. He keeps things. He's kept me in a drawer for fifty years.

30:4.9.7.text: I told you. A truck crew. Ours. They radioed the camp. I went. Eino's jacket was on the landing rock, folded. Folded, like you'd fold it to sit on. The deputy came out at noon. Dale Sorensen drove up behind him, the office's man, in a clean shirt. He stood on the rock with his hands in his pockets. The deputy asked me was Eino a careful man. Dale was standing next to me. I said, 'He was a careful man.' That's all I said. Five words. I didn't say the jacket. I didn't say the wind. Ollie said the wind. Ollie's a better man than me.

30:4.9.8.text: The ninth of September, '77. Here. Dale's truck was parked where my pickup is. Walt went to it in the middle of the afternoon, opened the door, took out a green book and a folder, and walked to his own truck. He saw me see him. I went back in the shed. I never said a word. Not to Dale, not to Brekke when he tore the office apart, not to anybody. The one thing I did right in that whole business, I did by keeping my mouth shut. Same as all the wrong ones. You see the trouble.

30:4.9.9.text: December. The Legion. Walt came and sat next to me at the bar. He didn't order. He said, 'Tell Dale this.' And I did. Word for word. I've never said it since. 'If I go in the water, it all comes up. Leave my mother alone and it stays down.' Dale listened and paid for my beer. And nobody went to Helmi's kitchen again. And nothing came up. Forty years. I was the mailman for the deal that let them off. That's what I did.

30:4.9.10.text: Because Walt went in the water. Birch. South shore. Upwind. And nothing came up. That was the deal, and he broke it on purpose, and he did it so I'd know. He was telling me the deal's off. Telling me. I'm the one who carried it. And then nobody came. Seven years. I did the porches every summer and nobody came. And then you walked out of a store with fourteen on your back.

30:4.9.c8.text: When it comes to it, will you say this to someone who'll write it down?

30:4.9.11.text: Clean book and all. My hand's in both of them. Theirs and his. Eino's books and Brekke's book, both in my hand. Somebody'd have to say how that happened, or it reads like I did it all. If it comes to that. If.

30:4.9.12.text: That's kind. It's not true, but it's kind.

30:4.9.c11.text: Tauno recopied three days of the 1976 readings into a clean book for Brekke. His hand on their numbers.

30:4.9.c12.text: Tauno reached the landing rock first and saw Eino's jacket folded there. The deputy came at noon, Sorensen behind him. With Sorensen at his elbow, Tauno told the deputy only 'He was a careful man.'

30:4.9.c13.text: 9 Sep 1977: Walt took a green book and a folder from Sorensen's truck at the crew camp. Tauno saw.

30:4.9.c14.text: Dec 1977: Walt's message to Sorensen, through Tauno: 'If I go in the water, it all comes up. Leave my mother alone and it stays down.'

30:4.9.c15.text: Tauno read Walt's canoe as 'the deal's off'.

30:4.9.15.text: I slept. Can you believe that. Eight hours.

30:4.10.5.text: Huh. He carries it like he still is.

30:4.10.c3.text: Did you ever say anything? About the old stations?

30:4.10.8.text: I said so. In writing. Last year. I was told it's a closed question. I still have the note. Don't ask me for it. I'm saying I have it.

30:4.10.w1.text: Tasha flagged the 1976 'background' stations in writing in 2025. Told it's a closed question.

30:5.1.text: I never wrote anything for them.

30:5.2.text: Kettle pad's up by the river, north of Gabbro.

30:5.3.text: Nothing was ever drilled east of Bald Eagle.

30:5.4.text: Walt was never right after his brother.

30:5.7.text: I go every day but Thursday.

30:5.8.text: I just typed. I never read what I typed.

30:8.2.1.text: My numbers are in a drawer. They're using his.
